articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting Requirements
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning the blocking and rejecting of transactions, as well as the associated reporting requirements.

These amendments aim to provide updated guidance to financial institutions and other entities on their obligations under OFAC sanctions programs. The changes are crucial for ensuring compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations and preventing illicit financial activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran-Related Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, and Releases General Licenses
body: OFAC has announced new designations related to Iran, alongside the removal of certain designations pertaining to Belarus and North Korea. This action reflects ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy in response to evolving geopolitical landscapes.

In conjunction with these changes, OFAC has also issued new general licenses related to Iran and Russia, and amended existing Frequently Asked Questions. These licenses aim to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, providing clarity and flexibility for specific activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) Designations with Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations target entities and individuals involved in activities that undermine American intellectual property rights.

To mitigate unintended consequences, OFAC has also issued associated general licenses. These licenses provide specific authorizations for certain transactions that might otherwise be impacted by the PAIPA designations, ensuring that legitimate activities can continue.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: OFAC has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This update provides clarification and potential adjustments to existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Venezuela.
The amendment aims to refine the scope of permissible activities under the Venezuela sanctions program, reflecting ongoing policy considerations and humanitarian concerns.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba Entities, Issues New and Amended General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting entities and individuals related to Iran and Cuba. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter illicit activities and support U.S. foreign policy objectives.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC has issued new and amended general licenses, along with updated Frequently Asked Questions. These measures aim to provide guidance and authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, ensuring clarity for affected parties.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation. This action indicates a recalibration of sanctions against certain individuals or entities associated with Venezuela.
Such removals can signify a shift in policy or a determination that the designated party no longer meets the criteria for inclusion on the sanctions list.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting illicit networks globally.

These designations aim to sever financial ties and limit the operational capabilities of those supporting drug trafficking and terrorist organizations. The action was undertaken in coordination with multiple U.S. law enforcement agencies and Mexico's Financial Intelligence Unit.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million Over Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has reached a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., totaling $11,662,930. The settlement addresses apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those targeting Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

Bank of America processed millions of dollars in payments in apparent violation of these sanctions programs. OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, resulting in no reduction to the base penalty.

body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics. Details of the settlement were not immediately available but are typically related to apparent violations of U.S. sanctions programs.

In separate actions, OFAC has also designated entities related to the International Criminal Court and issued associated general licenses. Additionally, a Burma-related designation has been removed, indicating a review and adjustment of sanctions against specific parties.

General Licenses are often issued to facilitate specific types of humanitarian aid, journalistic activities, or other transactions deemed to be in the U.S. national interest, or to clarify the scope of existing sanctions.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Civil Money Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for widespread breakdowns in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance program. This is the largest civil money penalty in OCC history.

The OCC found that the bank's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, with a transaction monitoring system that failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions. This resulted in the bank filing a large number of late suspicious activity reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars.

This action was taken in coordination with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), which assessed a $1.2 billion fine that credits the OCC's $750 million penalty. The OCC emphasized that banks of Bank of America's size and complexity must devote sufficient resources to ensure compliance with laws designed to detect and prevent money laundering.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express National Bank for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has issued a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank for significant deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance program.

The OCC determined that the bank failed to establish and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program reasonably designed to assure and monitor compliance with the BSA and its implementing regulations. Deficiencies included inadequate resources, systemic internal control gaps, weak independent testing, and insufficient BSA/AML training.

The bank's BSA/AML risk assessment focused on its demand deposit business, insufficiently addressing the risks in its more dominant credit and charge card products. These failures contributed to the bank's inability to timely identify and report approximately $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity over the past decade.

articles.headline: OCC Issues Prohibition Order Against Jennifer Hamblin for Embezzlement
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has issued an Order of Prohibition against Jennifer Hamblin, a former Vault Teller at a Cincinnati, Ohio, branch of Fifth Third Bank, N.A. The order stems from Hamblin's embezzlement of customer funds, which resulted in a loss of approximately $292,000 for the bank.

Prohibition orders are issued by the OCC to prevent individuals from participating in the affairs of any bank or other institution as defined in 12 USC 1818(e)(7), reinforcing accountability for individual conduct within the banking sector.

articles.headline: OCC Issues Prohibition Order Against Christopher Organista for Embezzlement of Customer Funds

Organista was found to have embezzled approximately $194,131 in bank customer funds.
This enforcement action highlights the OCC's commitment to deterring and correcting violations, unsafe or unsound practices, and breaches of fiduciary duty by institution-affiliated parties.

articles.headline: BIS Adds Over Three Dozen Entities to Entity List, Citing National Security Concerns
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has announced the addition of 37 parties to its Entity List, citing reasonable cause to believe they are involved in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States. The majority of these additions (28) are from China, with others from Belarus, Burma, Pakistan, Russia, and Taiwan.

Entities on the Entity List are subject to restrictive licensing requirements and policies, significantly impacting their ability to acquire U.S.-origin items. BIS also modified the license review policy of a prominent Chinese university to a presumption of denial due to its contributions to China's military modernization efforts.

This action underscores BIS's continued focus on preventing the diversion of U.S. technology to unauthorized end-users and end-uses, particularly in areas related to advanced computing and military modernization.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.

articles.headline: Sydney's new $5bn airport has one big problem: Getting there is tough
body: The airport won’t have direct public transportation for a year. How do locals feel about getting there?

articles.headline: Watch: How President Lula turned it around to beat Flávio Bolsonaro
body: Brazil's left-wing President has been elected for a fourth term after narrowly beating right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro in a knife-edge vote.

articles.headline: Why Israel's election is one of the most important in its history
body: Security and democracy emerge as central issues in Israel's highly anticipated general election, as Middle East correspondent Lucy Williamson reports.

articles.headline: Fireworks and tear gas as protesters and riot police clash in Paris
body: The BBC's Europe correspondent reports from Paris where mostly peaceful protests turned into unrest after nightfall.

articles.headline: Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global
body: The next fortnight sees two elections on different continents. The outcomes will shape geopolitics and the global economy, writes James Landale
